1. Global Homicide Rate Overview

The core question this report addresses is whether the world is becoming safer from intentional homicide. The global median homicide rate based on the most recent available data per country stands at 2.58 per 100,000 population, while the mean is 7.47 — the gap between these two measures indicates significant rightward skew, driven by a small number of countries with very high rates.

Key Finding The global mean homicide rate has declined across successive decades. However, the improvement is uneven — the median has been more stable, suggesting that while extreme rates have moderated, the typical country's experience has changed less dramatically.

Reporting Coverage

Data coverage varies significantly over time. Earlier years have fewer reporting countries, which can bias trend interpretation. The chart below shows the number of countries with available data by year.

Data Caveat The composition of reporting countries changes from year to year. A rising or falling average may partly reflect which countries are included, not just genuine rate changes. Caution is warranted when interpreting year-to-year movements, especially before 2000 where coverage is thinner.

3. Gender Disparity in Homicide Victimization

One of the most striking features of global homicide data is the persistent gender gap. Men are far more likely to die by homicide than women in virtually every country. The global median male-to-female homicide rate ratio is 3.2x as of 2023, meaning the typical country's male homicide rate is roughly 3 times its female rate.

Critical Insight The male-to-female ratio of approximately 3:1 is one of the most robust findings in criminology. While both sexes have experienced declining rates over time, the disparity has remained remarkably persistent. This has profound implications for targeted violence prevention — policies that fail to account for the gendered nature of homicide risk will miss the population most affected.

4. Age Group Analysis

Homicide risk is not uniformly distributed across age groups. Young adults consistently face the highest rates of homicide victimization worldwide, while children and the elderly are at comparatively lower risk.

Age Group Trends

Key Finding The 20–24 and 25–29 age groups consistently exhibit the highest homicide rates globally, followed closely by the 18–19 and 30–44 groups. This pattern aligns with broader criminological research identifying young adulthood as the period of highest victimization risk. Policy interventions targeting this demographic — including community-based violence prevention, employment programs, and conflict mediation — may yield the greatest impact.

6. Data Limitations & Policy Recommendations

Data Limitations

  • Unbalanced panel: This dataset is an unbalanced panel — not all countries report data for every year. The number of reporting countries varies from as few as 84 to as many as 162. Trend analyses may be influenced by changes in the composition of reporting countries over time.
  • Reporting gaps: 201 unique countries appear in the dataset, but no country has complete coverage for all 34 years. Missing data reflects gaps in national statistical capacity and reporting systems, not zero homicide rates.
  • United Kingdom caveat: UK data refers to England and Wales only. Scotland and Northern Ireland may appear as separate entries and should not be aggregated with the UK figure.
  • Territories: Some territories (e.g., Hong Kong, Macao, Puerto Rico) are reported separately. These should not be double-counted with their parent countries in aggregate analyses.
  • Definition consistency: While UNODC strives for consistent definitions of "intentional homicide," legal definitions vary across jurisdictions. What counts as intentional homicide in one country may be classified differently in another.
  • Underreporting: Countries with weak rule of law or limited statistical infrastructure may underreport homicides. The observed rates should be considered lower bounds for such countries.

Policy Recommendations

1. Invest in data infrastructure The most fundamental constraint on evidence-based homicide policy is data quality. International partners should support capacity-building for civil registration and vital statistics systems, particularly in regions with the largest reporting gaps.
2. Target young adult males The 18–29 age group faces homicide rates far exceeding other demographics. Violence prevention programs — including community mediation, employment initiatives, and substance abuse treatment — should prioritize this population. The persistent 3:1 male-to-female ratio demands gender-responsive strategies.
3. Learn from outlier improvements Countries that have achieved dramatic reductions in homicide rates (e.g., American Samoa, Isle of Man, Singapore) offer case studies for evidence-based intervention. International knowledge-sharing platforms should facilitate the transfer of successful strategies across contexts.
4. Monitor deteriorating situations Countries experiencing sharp increases in homicide rates require urgent attention. Rapid assessment and targeted intervention — including rule-of-law strengthening, organized crime disruption, and community-based prevention — can prevent further deterioration.
5. Account for regional disparities Global averages mask enormous regional variation. Policymakers should use region-specific baselines and targets rather than global benchmarks. Resource allocation for violence prevention should be proportional to regional burden.
